title: The Lapita expansion, the Bismarcks to Samoa, c. 1500–800 BC
summary: The makers of dentate-stamped Lapita pottery spread from the Bismarck Archipelago through the Solomons, Vanuatu and New Caledonia to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa in some six or seven centuries: the first people anywhere to settle islands beyond sight of land, sailing upwind into the trade winds.

legs.source: the dated Lapita sites (Denham, Bronk Ramsey and Specht 2012; Burley); the way between them is the usual drawing, not a recorded course
the Lapita sites of New Caledonia (Foué, Koné), a side branch off the main stream

events.label: Talepakemalai, Mussau
events.text: The oldest Lapita site known. The stamped pottery appears here with no local forerunner. Whether it begins nearer 1500 or 1300 BC is still argued.

events.label: Watom, off New Britain
events.text: Early Lapita settlement in the Bismarcks. Whether this first stage was a fast "express train" out of island Southeast Asia or a slow mingling with the people already there is one of the long arguments of Pacific archaeology.

events.label: Nenumbo, Reef Islands
events.text: Past the main Solomons into Remote Oceania, the islands nobody had reached before. From here on, every island was settled across open sea.

events.label: Teouma, Efate
events.text: A Lapita cemetery with headless burials, the skulls taken away and some later set on the chests of others. The ancient DNA from it shows the first settlers were mostly of East Asian ancestry; Papuan ancestry came later.

events.label: Foué and Koné, New Caledonia
events.text: Lapita reached New Caledonia from Vanuatu. The culture takes its name from a site here, Lapita near Koné, dug in 1952.

events.label: Natunuku and Bourewa, Viti Levu
events.text: The first settlement of Fiji, across some 850 km of open sea east of Vanuatu.

events.label: Nukuleka, Tongatapu
events.text: The first known settlement in Polynesia. A date of 1500 BC for Fiji or Tonga, still met with, is too early.

events.label: Mulifanua, ʻUpolu, Samoa
events.text: The one Lapita site in Samoa, drowned under the ferry berth and found when it was dredged. Here the stream stopped for nearly two thousand years.
